data.title: Course map, sources, and how to use this manual
data.subtitle: Introduction to the Computer Science C course

narr: Welcome to the Computer Science course focusing on programming in C.
This manual covers weeks 4 through 7 of the Foundations of Computer Science track at Tashkent University of Technology.
The course is structured in four layers: weekly lectures, laboratory exercises, bug hunt worksheets, and a coffee machine project.
Let's explore how this manual is organized and how you can make the most of it.
The course consists of four main components.
First, there are weekly lectures that review previous topics and introduce new ones.
Second, laboratory exercises based on specific textbook chapters with CS50 input helpers.
Third, bug hunt worksheets focusing on finding errors in conditional constructs, functions, loops, pointers, and strings.
Finally, the coffee machine project files, particularly the week 6 model with Stock, Recipe, and Cup components.
The manual covers material from weeks 4 through 7, focusing on several key programming concepts in C.
These include data types and operators, which form the foundation of variable manipulation.
Control structures that determine program flow, including conditionals and loops.
Functions and structures that help organize code into reusable components.
And finally, pointers, strings, and recursion which are more advanced C concepts.
Each week corresponds to a specific set of files in the course folder.
Lectures are held on Tuesdays, while labs follow the textbook chapter structure.
Let's examine how the materials are organized across these four weeks.
Here's the weekly breakdown of topics and corresponding files.
Week 4 focuses on data types and operators, with lecture4.txt and Week4.txt as primary materials.
Week 5 covers control structures, including branching and loops, with additional bug hunt files.
Week 6 deals with functions and structures, including the coffee machine project.
Finally, week 7 explores pointers, strings, and recursion with lecture and additional materials.

data.title: Week 4 — Data Types and Operators
data.subtitle: Foundation of the C programming course

narr: Week 4 establishes the foundation for the entire C programming course.
We'll explore C variables, data types, their sizes and precision.
The week covers various operators including arithmetic, logical, and bitwise operations.
Additionally, we'll examine increment/decrement, compact assignment, ternary operators, type conversions, and operator precedence.
The laboratory exercises include sphere precision, leap year rule, memory bridge, and alphabetical join tasks.

data.heading: C Language Characteristics
bullets: Used for systems programming (compilers, OS, DBMS, microcontrollers)
Weakly typed (allows implicit conversions and casting)

narr: C is a programming language with several key characteristics.
It's fast, small, universal, and platform-independent, making it suitable for various applications.
C is primarily used for systems programming, including compilers, operating systems, database management systems, and microcontrollers.
It's a statically typed, compiled language that follows structured and imperative programming paradigms.
Importantly, C is weakly typed, meaning it allows implicit conversions and potentially dangerous type casting.

data.heading: C Data Types
bullets: Data type determines values and operations

narr: C has a small family of data types that form the building blocks of programs.
These include numeric types like int, float, and double for different kinds of numbers.
Character type (char) for storing single characters.
And user-defined types like struct and union for creating complex data structures.
The data type of an object in memory determines both the set of values it can take and the operations that can be applied to it.

data.text: C is quirky, flawed, and an enormous success

narr: As Dennis Ritchie, the creator of C, once said:
"C is quirky, flawed, and an enormous success."
This quote captures both the imperfections and the remarkable impact of C on computer science.
